title: Purpose
summary: Who this design system serves. Answer this scope first.

questions.prompt: What kind of product is this system for?
questions.summary: Product type changes density, type, and color later.

options.label: Dense data
options.summary: Tables, tools, and other high-information screens.
options.why: Tables, tools and other screens that carry a lot of information. You get compact rows and tight space.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if people scan many rows and stay in the product for long stretches.
trade_offs: Alerts and messages can be harder to notice and read
Touch targets must still be at least 48 px

sources.name: Material
sources.title: Using Material density on the web

recommends.question: spacing-base
recommends.reason: A fine 4 px base keeps dense screens aligned.

options.label: Content
options.why: Pages people come to read. You get comfortable type, clear contrast and room around the text.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if people come to read pages, not to run a tool.
trade_offs: Dense screens can feel sparse

recommends.question: line-height
recommends.reason: Body copy gets room to breathe with a 1.5 line height.

discourages.question: density
discourages.reason: Pages people read need room around the text, so compact density works against that.

options.label: Commerce
options.summary: A shop or other purchase flow.
options.why: A shop or other purchase flow. You get clear actions, readable prices and a brand color people can recognize.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if people compare products and then buy.
trade_offs: A lot of color can distract from the task

sources.name: Shopify Help
sources.title: Customizing the style of your checkout

options.label: Calm
options.why: A low-pressure product. You get fewer accents, more space and a quiet voice.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if the product should feel slow and low pressure.
trade_offs: Urgent tasks can look understated

discourages.question: density
discourages.reason: Compact density leaves less room, which works against a calm, low-pressure page.

options.label: Consumer
options.summary: Short sessions for a broad audience.
options.why: A product used in short sessions by a broad audience that did not come looking for a tool.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if the audience is broad and sessions are short.
trade_offs: Expert users may want more density

questions.why_care: It says what the system is for, and it points at density, space, and line height.

questions.prompt: Who is the primary user, and what is the context?
questions.summary: Say who uses the system and in what situation.

options.label: Public visitors
options.why: People arrive without training and decide fast. The first screen has to make sense on its own.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if most people are not signed in.
trade_offs: You explain more on every page

options.label: Operators
options.summary: People who use the product often.
options.why: People who use the product often and learn its patterns. You can lean on that familiarity.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if trained people use it most days.
trade_offs: New visitors get less explanation

options.label: Mixed
options.why: Some people visit once and others work in the product every day. One system serves both.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if visitors and operators share one system.
trade_offs: One density will not fit both groups well

questions.prompt: What accessibility target do you commit to?
questions.summary: The target is a commitment. It does not calculate contrast.

options.label: WCAG 2.2 AA
options.summary: The common target for text and UI parts.
options.why: WCAG 2.2 level AA is a common target for text and interface parts. You get clear targets, such as 4.5:1 contrast for body text.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if you need to meet AA and AAA is not required yet.
trade_offs: Some large text can still be hard to read
Very light brand colors may not pass

recommends.question: contrast-metric
recommends.reason: A target that names WCAG 2.2 pairs with the WCAG contrast metric.

recommends.question: contrast-check
recommends.reason: Level AA can be reviewed once the color values are written.

options.label: WCAG 2.2 AAA
options.why: Level AAA asks for stronger contrast than AA, such as 7:1 for body text. You get a stricter target.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if your audience needs the stricter contrast target.
trade_offs: Brand colors get harder to keep

recommends.question: contrast-metric
recommends.reason: The stricter target still uses the WCAG contrast metric.

recommends.question: contrast-check
recommends.reason: Level AAA is easier to keep when the scale itself promises contrast.

questions.why_care: It sets the WCAG 2.2 floor your contrast checks have to meet.

questions.prompt: Which platforms does this system serve?
questions.summary: The platform changes units and components.

options.label: Web
options.why: A website or web app. With rem units, type follows the reader's own font settings.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if the system ships in a browser first.
trade_offs: Native apps need a later pass

recommends.question: css-unit
recommends.reason: On the web, rem lets type follow the reader's own font size.

options.label: Native
options.why: iOS, Android or desktop apps. On Apple platforms, screens use the San Francisco system font and the recommended text sizes.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if there is no website in this version.
trade_offs: Web visitors are out of scope

options.label: Web and native
options.why: One system serves a website and native apps. You share tokens in DTCG format and keep the structure steady.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if both surfaces ship from the same decisions.
trade_offs: You keep two sets of components

questions.prompt: What is the team size and maturity?
questions.summary: How many people maintain the system, and how established is the practice.

options.label: Solo, starting
options.summary: One person is setting the system up.
options.why: One person is starting the system. Fewer choices are easier to keep true.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if one person maintains the system.
trade_offs: Later teams may need more written rules

options.label: Small practiced team
options.summary: A few people edit the system.
options.why: A few people edit the system and can review a short list of decisions together.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if a few people edit the system each week.
trade_offs: A larger program will outgrow the short list

options.label: Large established team
options.summary: Many people ship from the system.
options.why: Many people ship from the system. Named owners and locked choices help files stay in step.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if many people ship UI from this system.
trade_offs: A change takes longer to agree

recommends.question: locked-at-init
recommends.reason: When many people ship from one system, locking core names after setup keeps files in step.

questions.prompt: Is this a single brand or more than one?
questions.summary: Multi-brand needs structure and theme to stay apart.

options.label: Single brand
options.why: One brand and one theme. Components can still keep structure apart from values.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if you will not ship a second brand soon.
trade_offs: A second brand later means a new theme pass

options.label: Multi-brand
options.summary: Two or more brands share components.
options.why: Two or more brands share components, and only the theme values change.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if two brands must use the same components.
trade_offs: Components cannot hold color values themselves

recommends.question: structure-theme-separation
recommends.reason: Two brands can share components only when theme values stay outside the components.

questions.why_care: It decides whether one brand owns the theme or several brands share the components.

questions.prompt: What data does the interface mostly show?
questions.summary: The kind of data changes how much should fit on one screen.
questions.why_care: The kind of data decides how much fits on a screen.

options.label: Text
options.why: Long writing needs room. Compact rows make a paragraph harder to read.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if people read paragraphs more than they scan rows.
trade_offs: A dense table shows fewer rows.

options.label: Metrics, prices and charts
options.summary: Figures people compare, not rows of records.
options.why: Metrics and charts need clear figures. They are not a list of records.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if the screen is prices, metrics, or charts.
trade_offs: Record lists may feel sparse.

options.label: Media
options.why: Pictures and video need space around the frame. Tight rows fight the image.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if images or video are the main content.
trade_offs: Tools get less room on screen.

options.label: Mixed
options.summary: More than one kind of content.
options.why: More than one kind of data shares the screen. One density will not fit all.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if no single kind of data dominates.
trade_offs: One density is a compromise.

options.label: Tables and lists of records
options.why: A table of records needs many rows in view. Compact space shows more of them.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if people scan rows of records.
trade_offs: Long reading becomes harder.

recommends.question: density
recommends.reason: Data-dense tables need many rows in view in order to show the most information in limited space, so your system will use compact density.

questions.prompt: How dense should the interface feel?
questions.summary: Density is the amount of space around controls and text.

options.label: Compact
options.why: Compact density fits more on a screen. It suits tools and tables.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if people need many controls in view.
trade_offs: Long reading gets tiring

questions.prompt: What voice and personality should the words have?
questions.summary: Voice is how the interface speaks. It is not a color.

options.label: Plain
options.why: Clear words and little personality. Say the action and stop.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if clarity matters more than personality.
trade_offs: The brand can sound flat

options.label: Warm
options.why: Human and direct, without slang. It does not joke about the task.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if you want a human tone without slang.
trade_offs: Serious errors can sound too soft

recommends.question: chroma-hue-shift
recommends.reason: A warm voice pairs with darker color steps that shift a little warmer.

options.label: Precise
options.why: Exact names and clear next steps, with no filler.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if experts need exact labels.
trade_offs: New people may find it cold
